Musk and Altman both read the DeepMind sale the same way: one company was going to own the best AI lab on earth. OpenAI was founded as the counterweight — a nonprofit, publishing openly, funded by a billion dollars in pledges. The founding is a direct reaction to this purchase.
The nonprofit that was meant to prevent concentration could not agree on who ran it. Musk's bid for control failed, he left the board, and most of the pledged money never arrived.
With the founding money gone and training costs climbing, a nonprofit could not buy compute. The capped-profit subsidiary and the Microsoft deal exist because the original funding model collapsed.

Weizenbaum's warning was that people read minds into pattern-matching. Fifty-six years later a professional engineer, with access to the weights, did exactly that.
Both events answer the same question — what happens when internal safety criticism collides with product pressure. One ended in a firing; the other in a rival company.

A nonprofit board with a duty to humanity now sat on top of a company worth tens of billions to its investors and staff. When the board finally used its power, the commercial side simply out-voted it with resignation letters.
The chief scientist backed the removal and lost. Six months later he was gone and the long-horizon safety team he co-led no longer existed.
